title: Pressure dependence of surface tension of polymer melts under high vacuum

paper_content.abstract:
The surface tension of polymers under ambient or high-pressure conditions has been
extensively studied but is less explored under high vacuum. Here, the effect of air pressure on the
surface tension of polymer melts is studied by using a home-built apparatus. While previous
studies showed that the surface tension of most polymers decreases linearly when the temperature
or pressure is increased, we show that the surface tension of polymer is found to exhibit an
anomalous behavior: The surface tension remains a decreasing function of the temperature, but
increases with increasing air pressure. The measured surface tension of several polymer samples
is well described by the Hill equation in the pressure range of 10−4 to 105 N/m2. The implication
of this behavior on the air-polymer interaction is discussed within the context of air adsorption
paper_content.introduction:
The surface tension (𝛾) of polymer melts is an important property of polymeric materials and
plays a key role in numerous engineering processes, such as polymer blending1, polymer foaming2,
wetting3, and particles or fiber dispersion in polymers4. Naturally, the surface tension of polymers
depends on the thermodynamic conditions, commonly specified by the temperature (𝑇) and
pressure (𝑃). It is well-established that the surface tension of most polymer melts decreases slightly
with the temperature, following approximately a linear relationship, at ambient pressure of the
order of 105 Pa5-10. Similarly, the pressure dependence of 𝛾, determined under high-pressure
conditions, was observed to decrease linearly when the pressure is increased at a constant
temperature11-18. The decrease of 𝛾 with increasing 𝑃 is attributed to either increased gas
dissolution or the reduction of density difference between the two phases across the interface11-18.
However, the pressure dependence of 𝛾 under high vacuum conditions has not been studied prior
to the current work.

In contrast to the abundant studies under ambient or high-pressure, the phase behaviors of
polymers and their surface tension under high vacuum conditions have attracted much less
attention, largely due to the difficulty of precisely controlling pressure to reach high vacuum
conditions. Recently, it has been discovered that placing diblock copolymers under high vacuum
conditions could lead to a drastic orientation change from parallel to perpendicular for the self-
assembled cylindrical nanostructure19. The origin of this interesting discovery could be attributed
to a much-reduced surface tension difference between the different blocks, i.e. polystyrene (PS)
and polydimethylsiloxane (PDMS) or poly(L-lactide) (PLLA), under high vacuum20,21. While it is
natural to suggest that the surface tensions of the polymers depend on the pressure, a systematic
study, quantitatively or even qualitatively, of the effect of air pressure on the surface tension of
polymers has been lacking. Here, we fill this gap by carrying out a systematic study of the effect
of air pressure on the surface tension of polymer melts under high vacuum. Specifically, we
designed and constructed a homemade vacuum oven (Supplementary Figure. 1) that enabled us to
achieve a high vacuum and measured the surface tension of polymer melts by the pre-coated
capillary height method. It is noted that several techniques, such as pendant, sessile, spinning drop,
etc. could be used to obtain the surface tension. These methods have the advantage of requiring a
minimum amount of sample and are applicable to various cases22-24. However, their performance
and sensitivity significantly decrease when the drop shape becomes nearly spherical25,26. In the
current study, the pre-coated capillary technique was chosen due to its simplicity and reliability20.
We carried out surface tension measurements on several representative polymer samples,
including polyethylene glycol (PEG), polyisoprene (PI), polypropylene (PP), PS, and PDMS, with
a wide range of surface tension values under ambient conditions. A very surprising observation
from our study is that, in contrast to the pressure effect on the surface tension under ambient or
high-pressure, the surface tension of all the polymers exhibits a significant decrease when the
pressure drops below 103 N/m2. This anomalous behavior of the polymer surface tension must be
related to the polymer-air interactions. This new finding reveals interesting physics at the air-
polymer interfaces and, furthermore, sheds light on potential applications of designing polymeric
materials for nanopatterning technologies within nano-microelectronic manufacturing systems
(MEMS).

Temperature Dependence of Surface Tension
To explore the temperature dependence of surface tension for polymeric melts, systematic
measurements were carried out using a homemade vacuum oven apparatus. As a validation of our
experimental method, the surface tension of the polymer samples (shown in Fig. 1) was obtained
as a function of temperature in the range from 170 to 220°C, under ambient pressure (~105 N/m2).
It is noted that the surface tension data for PS and PDMS were reported in our previous work20.
The data for PI was not available for temperatures over 200°C due to thermal degradation of the
sample. In agreement with the literature5-10, the measured surface tension shown in Fig. 1 for the
five polymers (PEG, PS, PI, PP, and PDMS) exhibits a slight linear decrease when the temperature
is increased, with a slope in the range of -0.08 to -0.12. The agreement between the results from
the current study and the literature validates our experimental methods.

Pressure Dependence of Surface Tension
Several previous studies have demonstrated a small reduction in surface tension at high
pressure and temperature. However, there has been less focus on the low-pressure region. To fill
this gap, we carried out measurements of polymer surface tension under low-pressure conditions.
The homemade oven allowed us to access low-pressure conditions, thus enabling the measurement
of the surface tension under high vacuum conditions. Specifically, surface tension of several
sample polymers was obtained in the pressure range from atmospheric pressure (105 N/m2) to 10-
4 N/m2. The measured surface tension of the samples at a temperature of 200°C are presented in
Table 1, revealing a clear decrease in surface tension with decreasing air pressure. Interestingly, a
drastic reduction in surface tension is observed as the pressure drops below atmospheric levels
(105 N/m2). Since the pressure change was over 8 orders of magnitude, a linear plot of our data
compresses most of the points to a vertical line. Instead, it is the best to use log-linear plot to
demonstrate the change of the measured surface tension. The data points and their best fitting by
Hill equation as shown in Fig. 2. It is important to mention that the trend of the surface tension
change is qualitatively different from the pressure effect under high-pressure conditions, where a
slight decrease of 𝛾 is observed when the pressure is increased11-18. Note that the low- and high-
pressure regimes involve distinct mechanisms. At low pressure, surface tension changes are
primarily governed by modifications in polymer–air interactions, as captured by the lattice model.
At high-pressure, the decrease in surface tension arises from gas dissolution or the reduced density
difference across the interface11,13.

To examine the generality of the observed behaviour, we measured the surface tension of two
polymers, PEG and PDMS, with different molecular weights under high vacuum conditions. These
two polymers were chosen because they possess the highest (PEG) and the lowest (PDMS) surface
tension under ambient conditions. Note that the PEG with a molecular weight (MW) of 20000
g/mol is referred to as PEG HMW and PEG with MW of 10000 g/mol molecular weight is referred
to as PEG LMW. Also, low MW (21,000 g/mol) PDMS is referred to as PDMS LMW and high
MW (38,000 g/mol) PDMS is referred to as PDMS HMW. As shown in Fig. 3, the molecular
weight of the polymers has a negligible effect on the surface tension. The observed pressure
dependence of surface tension is consistent across polymers of different molecular weights,
indicating that polymer chain length or PDI does not play a dominant role. Instead, the trend
primarily reflects intrinsic polymer-air interfacial interactions, suggesting that the pressure
dependence should be universal to polymers. It is plausible that the observed pressure dependence
of surface tension is not polymer-specific. Rather, it is the result of surface-air adsorption. In what
follows, we construct a theoretical model to understand and explain the observed temperature and
pressure dependence of the surface tension.

paper_content.methods:
Materials.
The polyethylene glycol (Mw = 20,000 g/mol, catalogue no. A17925.30) from Thermo
Scientific and polyethylene glycol (Mw = 10,000 g/mol, product no. P6667) from Sigma-Aldrich
used in this study were commercially available products. Polystyrene (Mw = 20,000 g/mol, PDI =
1.06), polyisoprene (Mw = 19,000 g/mol, PDI = 1.03), and polydimethylsiloxane (Mw = 21,000
and 38,000 g/mol, PDI = 1.09) were synthesized in the laboratory. Polypropylene (Mw = 12,000
g/mol, product no. 428116) used was a commercially available product and obtained from Sigma-
Aldrich.
The polymer samples, whether commercially obtained or prepared in the laboratory, were
used without additional processing such as solution casting or heat pressing. The samples were
either in powder form (e.g. PEG, PS, PP) or in viscous liquid-like form (e.g. PI and PDMS), and
were placed directly into clean glass vials. Each sample was placed in a clean glass vial along with
the suspended capillary tube and kept in a homemade vacuum oven. The rotary and diffusion pump
were operated overnight to achieve a high degree of vacuum in the chamber. Following this, the
oven was heated to the desired temperature while maintaining vacuum conditions. This process
enabled thermal annealing under high vacuum prior to testing.

Measurement of surface tension for polymeric melt
The surface tension measurements of representative polymeric systems were carried out using
the capillary rise method under zero-contact-angle conditions (See Supplementary information,
Pre-coated Capillary Height Method section for details). The dependence of surface tension on
thermodynamic variables like temperature and pressure was studied through experiments
conducted using a homemade vacuum oven apparatus, which was designed to precisely control
temperature and pressure conditions (See Supplementary Figure 1. for details). Five commonly
used polymers, including PDMS, PP, PI, PS, and PEG, ranging from low cohesive density to high
cohesive energy density, were employed in this study, and the values of surface tension at ambient
conditions are shown in Supplementary Table 1.

Data availability. The data that support the findings of this study are provided with this paper
and in the supplementary information. All additional data are available from the corresponding
author upon request.

reviewer_comments.reviewer_1:
In the manuscript, the authors measured the interfacial tension using the capillary height method. For a broad journal such as Nature Communications, the analysis of interfacial tension for the technique should be expanded on.
1. The authors propose a model that they claim captures the physics of changing interfacial tension as a function of pressure, but from what I could tell, they only used linear fits with two data points per line (Fig 5). If I am in error here, and more data points are used, the plot should be changed for clarity, since each line appears only to have 2-3 points over a broad pressure range. Furthermore, the cohesive energy of the polymers used is known; how do the cohesive energies extracted from this fit compare with literature values?
2. In Figure 2, the authors report an abrupt decrease when the air pressure drops below 103 Pa. However, only a single data point is provided above this threshold. Additional data points in that pressure range to support the observed trend.
3. Could the authors clarify the specific ranges defined as low pressure and high pressure in this study?
4. It is also suggested that the authors consider collecting surface tension data of the polymer melts under high pressure using the same method.
5. On page 5, the authors state: “A very interesting observation from this plot is the descending order of 1.65, 1.51, 1.25, 1.21, and 0.41 for PEG, PS, PI, PP, and PDMS, respectively.” Could the authors provide an explanation for this observed trend among the different polymers?
6. According to the fitting results (Table 1), the K value is 4 and appears to be invariant across different polymer types. Since the Langmuir constant (K) reflects the extent of interaction between the adsorbate and the surface, could the authors clarify whether the K value in Table 1 was derived from fitting or assumed? Additionally, could the authors explain why the K value remains constant across different polymers?
7. The authors suggest that the observed pressure effect should not be specific to polymers and should be universally applicable to any physiochemical systems. However, they do not provide any measurement data for other material types, such as ionic liquids, surfactants, or rigid molecules. Moreover, the lattice model and Langmuir isotherm employed appear overly simplistic. Polymers, particularly block copolymers, exhibit surface inhomogeneities and non-one-dimensional interfaces due to fluctuating chain ends, making the Langmuir adsorption isotherm an inadequate approximation for such systems.
8. The authors propose a model that they claim captures the physics of changing interfacial tension as a function of pressure, but from what I could tell, they only used linear fits with two data points per line (Fig 5). If I am in error here, and more data points are used, the plot should be changed for clarity, since each line appears only to have 2-3 points over a broad pressure range. Furthermore, the cohesive energy of the polymers used is known; how do the cohesive energies extracted from this fit compare with literature values?
9. The research is of broad interest, but I think some work needs to be done to validate their model of lowering interfacial tension due to gas adsorption.
Some further comments:
1. Page 5; last two sentences of 1st paragraph – “This could be presented better. The way this is worded now sounds like they are saying more than just the temperature change is varying the surface tension even though the pressure is being kept constant. I think they mean to say that the surface tension could be changed more dramatically by changing other factors, such as pressure.”
2. Page 5; middle of 2nd paragraph – “Should use a log scale for pressure in this graph to better illustrate this point because most of the important data points are overlapping significantly and the pressure at which the decrease happens isn’t obvious.”
3. Page 5; second to last sentence of 2nd paragraph – “Okay, so they do this in Figure 3 but why even include figure 2 then since it’s so unclear?”
4. Page 5; last sentence of 2nd paragraph – “What does this conclusion even mean? There are no units, and the plot doesn’t clearly reflect these values.” – I see now that they probably mean the slope values, but they don’t draw any conclusions about the significance of this decrease here or anywhere else in the manuscript.
5. Page 6; middle of 1st paragraph – “Normally I’d ask what the pdi is for each polymer here, but, since we’re dealing with a melt sample and the trend remains unchanged, perhaps it isn’t the most relevant. Depending on what’s said about the surface-air adsorption part of their theoretical model, the pdi may or may not be important to consider.”
6. Page 9; middle of 1st paragraph – “Is this for the same scenario (high-pressure) as the previous sentence?”
7. Page 10; end of 1st paragraph – “Back to my earlier point about pdi, perhaps pdi is contributing to this difference here since lower MWs preferentially locate at the surface and you cite air-polymer interactions at the interface to be the main contribution to the surface tension reduction. Also, what specifically is contributing to the differences in the slope values for each polymer?” – They should also mention why they think PI is different from the rest of the polymers.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_2:
The manuscript presents an interesting experimental study of the surface tension of polymer melts at low pressures. A threshold pressure is observed below which surface tension and pressure feature a strong positive correlation. To rationalize the existence of the pressure threshold the authors introduce a Langmuir isotherm model that justifies the existence of a critical pressure threshold with the hyperbolic shape of the isotherm.
Overall this is an interesting, innovative and well-executed study. Only few experimental studies of the surface tension of liquids (and polymers) have been reported in the low-pressure regime, thus there is potential that this study to stimulate follow-up work. It is noted that the performance of materials in low-pressure environments is increasingly receiving attention due to novel application demands, for example, in space exploration.
However, while I view this study very favorably overall, I am not compelled to recommend publication in Nature Communications. Although the study is pioneering in character, the scope is rather niche. Although the results could stimulate follow-up research in both fundamental and application-related areas for polymer materials, the focus of such activities is not elaborated in the proposal. There are also some 'loose ends' which leave the reader puzzled. For example, what is the role of chemistry on the observed differences between the different polymeric systems, molecular characteristics (for example, differences in dispersity indices) between the polymers are not mentioned. I did not find a description of the actual sample preparation process. For example, were materials solution processed or heat-pressed, where the materials, were materials conditioned by vacuum annealing prior to testing? It would have been interesting to evaluate for one chemistry the role of chain end density, for example, by variation of the molecular weight.
In summary, this is a high quality innovative work that deserves to be published in a specialized journal on polymer science.

reviewer_comments.reviewer_1:
The authors have made an interesting observation that the apparent interfacial tension decreases with decreasing pressure and that the reduction can be mapped on to a function put for by Hill to describe the behavior of receptors in biological systems. Here, the authors speculate that the surface of the molten polymers adsorb air molecules, and it is those adsorbed molecules that give rise to the observed variation in the apparent interfacial tension. Unlike biological systems where receptors have specific interactions, any interactions with the air molecules are left to the reader to decide. Air is a mixture of gases (78% N2, 21% O2 and 0.93% Ar). The authors make no attempt to discern between these and treat air as a single component gas, which it is not, nor do the authors perform any control experiments to differentiate between them. Certainly, there must be a difference between the adsorption of these different gases.
The master curve that the authors describe simply says that the functional form of the reduction is the same, suggesting, though not proving, that origin and mechanism of the adsorption is similar. Normalization of the data at the 50% change point, P0, and the range in the change of   ensures that the data will overlap. So, I am less impressed with the master curve and am still not informed as to the origin of the observation. Is it adsorption? Perhaps, but I would have expected some dependence on the chemical composition or the density of the polymer (free volume or concentration of chain ends at the surface or chain orientation at the surface or the interfacial tension of the specific polymer). None of these appear to be the case. So, what is it? The adsorption of interest is only at the surface, at least that is what will change the interfacial tension, but the surfaces of the different polymers are chemically different, have densities that are different and dynamics that will be different, but the measurements done here are insensitive to these differences. As I said in my earlier review, “I think some work needs to be done to validate their model of lowering interfacial tension due to gas adsorption.”, and I still feel that is the case. This work originated in the research that Ho had done on the orientation of block copolymer domains and there I could understand a preferential adsorption of any of a variety of vapors (gases, water vapor, or other gas) that could mediate the surface energies of the components. Yet, given the arguments the authors present in this manuscript, I am not certain that holds.
Consequently, even though I find the observations interesting, I do not feel that this manuscript has the scientific rigor for publication in Nature Comm. I strongly encourage the authors to pursue this further, since there will be some interesting physics underpinning the observed behavior, but I just do not see that in this manuscript.
As an aside, I do want to point out that S. Herminghaus and coworkers performed dome detailed studies on polymer thin films stability, dewetting, etc. where they also observed difference when the homopolymers and mixtures showed different behavior under vacuum or different gas atmospheres which they attributed to variation in the interfacial tensions and it would be worthwhile for the authors to look at his work.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_2: In my original review, I noted several points that needed revision prior to publication of the manuscript. The authors have expanded significant efforts to improve the quality of the original submission and I find that the revised manuscript comprehensively addresses all the points I raised (with the exception of principle suitability for Nature Commun). I commend the authors for significant extension of the data range, in particular, the study of M-dependence. I also appreciate the extended discussion of sample preparation procedures. While I remain skeptical about the suitability of such a narrow theme for a broad audience journal, the principal quality is now (in my opinion) on par with work that would generally be considered suitable for high impact broad audience journals. I have no further changes to suggest.

## Abstract

The surface tension of polymers under ambient or high-pressure conditions has been
extensively studied but is less explored under high vacuum. Here, the effect of air pressure on the
surface tension of polymer melts is studied by using a home-built apparatus. While previous
studies showed that the surface tension of most polymers decreases linearly when the temperature
or pressure is increased, we show that the surface tension of polymer is found to exhibit an
anomalous behavior: The surface tension remains a decreasing function of the temperature, but
increases with increasing air pressure. The measured surface tension of several polymer samples
is well described by the Hill equation in the pressure range of 10−4 to 105 N/m2. The implication
of this behavior on the air-polymer interaction is discussed within the context of air adsorption

---

## Introduction

The surface tension (𝛾) of polymer melts is an important property of polymeric materials and
plays a key role in numerous engineering processes, such as polymer blending1, polymer foaming2,
wetting3, and particles or fiber dispersion in polymers4. Naturally, the surface tension of polymers
depends on the thermodynamic conditions, commonly specified by the temperature (𝑇) and
pressure (𝑃). It is well-established that the surface tension of most polymer melts decreases slightly
with the temperature, following approximately a linear relationship, at ambient pressure of the
order of 105 Pa5-10. Similarly, the pressure dependence of 𝛾, determined under high-pressure
conditions, was observed to decrease linearly when the pressure is increased at a constant
temperature11-18. The decrease of 𝛾 with increasing 𝑃 is attributed to either increased gas
dissolution or the reduction of density difference between the two phases across the interface11-18.
However, the pressure dependence of 𝛾 under high vacuum conditions has not been studied prior
to the current work.

In contrast to the abundant studies under ambient or high-pressure, the phase behaviors of
polymers and their surface tension under high vacuum conditions have attracted much less
attention, largely due to the difficulty of precisely controlling pressure to reach high vacuum
conditions. Recently, it has been discovered that placing diblock copolymers under high vacuum
conditions could lead to a drastic orientation change from parallel to perpendicular for the self-
assembled cylindrical nanostructure19. The origin of this interesting discovery could be attributed
to a much-reduced surface tension difference between the different blocks, i.e. polystyrene (PS)
and polydimethylsiloxane (PDMS) or poly(L-lactide) (PLLA), under high vacuum20,21. While it is
natural to suggest that the surface tensions of the polymers depend on the pressure, a systematic
study, quantitatively or even qualitatively, of the effect of air pressure on the surface tension of
polymers has been lacking. Here, we fill this gap by carrying out a systematic study of the effect
of air pressure on the surface tension of polymer melts under high vacuum. Specifically, we
designed and constructed a homemade vacuum oven (Supplementary Figure. 1) that enabled us to
achieve a high vacuum and measured the surface tension of polymer melts by the pre-coated
capillary height method. It is noted that several techniques, such as pendant, sessile, spinning drop,
etc. could be used to obtain the surface tension. These methods have the advantage of requiring a
minimum amount of sample and are applicable to various cases22-24. However, their performance
and sensitivity significantly decrease when the drop shape becomes nearly spherical25,26. In the
current study, the pre-coated capillary technique was chosen due to its simplicity and reliability20.
We carried out surface tension measurements on several representative polymer samples,
including polyethylene glycol (PEG), polyisoprene (PI), polypropylene (PP), PS, and PDMS, with
a wide range of surface tension values under ambient conditions. A very surprising observation
from our study is that, in contrast to the pressure effect on the surface tension under ambient or
high-pressure, the surface tension of all the polymers exhibits a significant decrease when the
pressure drops below 103 N/m2. This anomalous behavior of the polymer surface tension must be
related to the polymer-air interactions. This new finding reveals interesting physics at the air-
polymer interfaces and, furthermore, sheds light on potential applications of designing polymeric
materials for nanopatterning technologies within nano-microelectronic manufacturing systems
(MEMS).

---

## Results

Temperature Dependence of Surface Tension
To explore the temperature dependence of surface tension for polymeric melts, systematic
measurements were carried out using a homemade vacuum oven apparatus. As a validation of our
experimental method, the surface tension of the polymer samples (shown in Fig. 1) was obtained
as a function of temperature in the range from 170 to 220°C, under ambient pressure (~105 N/m2).
It is noted that the surface tension data for PS and PDMS were reported in our previous work20.
The data for PI was not available for temperatures over 200°C due to thermal degradation of the
sample. In agreement with the literature5-10, the measured surface tension shown in Fig. 1 for the
five polymers (PEG, PS, PI, PP, and PDMS) exhibits a slight linear decrease when the temperature
is increased, with a slope in the range of -0.08 to -0.12. The agreement between the results from
the current study and the literature validates our experimental methods.

Pressure Dependence of Surface Tension
Several previous studies have demonstrated a small reduction in surface tension at high
pressure and temperature. However, there has been less focus on the low-pressure region. To fill
this gap, we carried out measurements of polymer surface tension under low-pressure conditions.
The homemade oven allowed us to access low-pressure conditions, thus enabling the measurement
of the surface tension under high vacuum conditions. Specifically, surface tension of several
sample polymers was obtained in the pressure range from atmospheric pressure (105 N/m2) to 10-
4 N/m2. The measured surface tension of the samples at a temperature of 200°C are presented in
Table 1, revealing a clear decrease in surface tension with decreasing air pressure. Interestingly, a
drastic reduction in surface tension is observed as the pressure drops below atmospheric levels
(105 N/m2). Since the pressure change was over 8 orders of magnitude, a linear plot of our data
compresses most of the points to a vertical line. Instead, it is the best to use log-linear plot to
demonstrate the change of the measured surface tension. The data points and their best fitting by
Hill equation as shown in Fig. 2. It is important to mention that the trend of the surface tension
change is qualitatively different from the pressure effect under high-pressure conditions, where a
slight decrease of 𝛾 is observed when the pressure is increased11-18. Note that the low- and high-
pressure regimes involve distinct mechanisms. At low pressure, surface tension changes are
primarily governed by modifications in polymer–air interactions, as captured by the lattice model.
At high-pressure, the decrease in surface tension arises from gas dissolution or the reduced density
difference across the interface11,13.

To examine the generality of the observed behaviour, we measured the surface tension of two
polymers, PEG and PDMS, with different molecular weights under high vacuum conditions. These
two polymers were chosen because they possess the highest (PEG) and the lowest (PDMS) surface
tension under ambient conditions. Note that the PEG with a molecular weight (MW) of 20000
g/mol is referred to as PEG HMW and PEG with MW of 10000 g/mol molecular weight is referred

used without additional processing such as solution casting or heat pressing. The samples were
either in powder form (e.g. PEG, PS, PP) or in viscous liquid-like form (e.g. PI and PDMS), and

the suspended capillary tube and kept in a homemade vacuum oven. The rotary and diffusion pump
were operated overnight to achieve a high degree of vacuum in the chamber. Following this, the
oven was heated to the desired temperature while maintaining vacuum conditions. This process
enabled thermal annealing under high vacuum prior to testing.

Measurement of surface tension for polymeric melt
The surface tension measurements of representative polymeric systems were carried out using
the capillary rise method under zero-contact-angle conditions (See Supplementary information,
Pre-coated Capillary Height Method section for details). The dependence of surface tension on
thermodynamic variables like temperature and pressure was studied through experiments
conducted using a homemade vacuum oven apparatus, which was designed to precisely control
temperature and pressure conditions (See Supplementary Figure 1. for details). Five commonly
used polymers, including PDMS, PP, PI, PS, and PEG, ranging from low cohesive density to high
cohesive energy density, were employed in this study, and the values of surface tension at ambient
conditions are shown in Supplementary Table 1.

Data availability. The data that support the findings of this study are provided with this paper
and in the supplementary information. All additional data are available from the corresponding
author upon request.
